ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Verify organic specialty case-count growth, unique customer growth, placement growth, acquisition integration, route optimization, gross-margin durability, and whether premium restaurant customers remain resilient despite traffic softness.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest filings and earnings-call data separating organic growth from M&A, validating case-count quality, customer retention, gross-margin durability, and whether demand is driven by resilient premium restaurant procurement rather than temporary pricing or acquisition mix.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Best Serenity fit in this chunk: a direct restaurant infrastructure beneficiary with specialty foodservice distribution exposure, premium independent restaurant customer relationships, fragmented-market roll-up potential, and route-density economics that can be tested through case growth, customer additions, gross margin, acquisition integration, and delivery productivity.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: It is not a consumer restaurant brand or mega-cap distributor; its value driver is hidden in specialty SKU access, chef relationships, local density, fragmented distribution consolidation, and premium restaurant procurement rather than obvious restaurant traffic headlines.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Verify sustained independent restaurant case growth, customer retention, digital ordering adoption, EBITDA per case, acquisition activity, and whether growth reflects share gains from smaller distributors.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need to separate broad restaurant demand recovery from true share gains, digital procurement monetization, EBITDA-per-case improvement, and customer mix quality.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Strong reference candidate for validating independent restaurant demand, broadline distributor route-density economics, digital ordering adoption, customer retention, and share gains from smaller distributors. It is less discovery-oriented than CHEF but offers clean public-market evidence for the foodservice distribution thesis.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Not truly underfollowed, but less consumer-facing than restaurant chains and useful as a scaled U.S. pure-play benchmark for independent restaurant case growth and distributor productivity.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Verify whether independent restaurant case volume, customer retention, private-label mix, delivery productivity, labor/fuel efficiency, and franchise-system partnerships are improving faster than restaurant traffic trends.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need segment-level proof that growth is driven by durable case-volume share gains, customer retention, productivity, and private-label economics rather than broad food-away-from-home inflation or temporary mix.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Primary reference leader for procurement scale, route density, food-safety resources, ordering infrastructure, and national restaurant supply-chain capability. Its evidence quality and falsifiability are high, but its underfollowed discovery and mispricing potential are lower because it is already widely recognized as the category leader.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Not underfollowed; included as the benchmark for route-density economics, national procurement scale, ordering infrastructure, franchise expansion support, and supplier/customer access.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Verify profitable route-density expansion, distribution-center utilization, customer retention, gross-margin recovery, cash conversion, debt/liquidity, auditor or governance flags, and whether the Asian restaurant distribution market remains fragmented enough for consolidation.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need current filings and governance review to verify cash conversion, customer retention, margin recovery, debt/liquidity, auditor issues, and whether the company has a durable ethnic foodservice distribution moat rather than generic low-margin wholesale exposure.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: High hidden-signal candidate because ethnic and cuisine-specific restaurant distribution may involve specialized SKUs, cultural/language selling, sticky customer relationships, and fragmented regional route density. However, it remains speculative because evidence quality, liquidity, governance, and operating-risk clarity are weaker than the distributor reference names.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Micro-cap scale, low liquidity, operational complexity, governance/history concerns, and classification as a small food wholesaler can keep it outside mainstream restaurant, logistics, and consumer screens.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Verify whether share gains come from regional roll-ups, specialty distribution, chain-customer wins, outsourcing by restaurant systems, gross-margin durability, and integration of acquisitions.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need current filings and earnings details showing whether growth is from durable national-chain wins, specialty distribution economics, acquisition synergies, or generic foodservice volume/pricing.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Useful reference comp for national-chain distribution, specialty distribution, convenience distribution, acquisition integration, and restaurant outsourcing economics. It scores well on route-density relevance and public-market purity but lower on underfollowed discovery because it is still a large-cap scaled distributor.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Less dominant in mainstream attention than Sysco, but still a large-cap reference name rather than a true discovery candidate; useful for studying national-chain distribution and consolidation dynamics.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Verify direct or indirect foodservice/restaurant exposure in filings, customer categories, product applications, channel partners, sanitation/cleaning SKUs, regulatory certifications, gross-margin improvement sustainability, and whether revenue is structurally tied to restaurant demand rather than generic industrial cycles.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need hard filing evidence tying revenue, customers, or product categories to restaurant sanitation, foodservice distribution, HI&I cleaning, food-contact compliance, or institutional foodservice demand.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: A low-ranking but potentially interesting second-order hypothesis. If direct restaurant, institutional sanitation, HI&I, distributor, or food-contact regulatory exposure is verified, it could become an obscure restaurant-infrastructure supplier. Current evidence is too weak to treat it as a confirmed restaurant chokepoint.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: It is screened as a small specialty chemical turnaround rather than a restaurant supplier; any restaurant linkage is likely buried inside HI&I, distributor, or institutional customer channels rather than disclosed as a clean restaurant segment.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Verify store-count growth, franchise pipeline, unit economics, liquidity, customer demand, dependence on Sysco distribution, product consistency, quality-control execution, and whether the partnership materially improves expansion economics.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need evidence that the Sysco partnership materially improves unit economics, franchise growth, product consistency, liquidity, and store-level profitability rather than simply supporting a high-risk micro-cap expansion story.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Included mainly as a speculative read-through on how emerging restaurant/franchise systems depend on scaled distribution, quality assurance, and supply-chain orchestration. It is not a strong chokepoint candidate because it is a tiny restaurant operator rather than an infrastructure supplier.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: It is a very small restaurant/franchise operator rather than a supplier chokepoint; included mainly as a speculative read-through on how distribution partnerships may enable emerging franchise systems.
